zones.label: Column 1

Supplied page subset used for entry identification, not as authority for this copy’s typography or spelling. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Transcription corrections and English notes are independently based on the supplied BnF scans.

runs.text: peçonha dentro do mel: diz ſe de hum homem

lines.note: Continues the preceding entry with the image of poison inside honey, applied to a person. The scan separates mel from diz ſe with a colon; the OCR reading mele dix obscured both the boundary and the verb.

runs.text: que de baixo de brandas palauras tem coração

lines.note: The relative clause describes someone who conceals a malicious heart beneath gentle words. Brandas palauras explains the honey metaphor on the preceding row.

runs.text: danado de matar, ou fazer outro mal.

lines.note: Completes the metaphor: the heart is bent on killing or doing other harm. This is the end of the carried-over explanation, not part of the following secret-communication entry.

Mittsuu is explained by hisoka ni tsuuzuru, communicating secretly. Both long-u marks are downward carons in this impression; the entry begins at the column margin rather than at continuation indentation.

runs.text: ſecretamente por recados, ou por cartas, ou

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies secret communication through messages or letters. Its final ou introduces the additional possibility on the next row.
Completes the means of secret communication: in some other manner. The short continuation belongs to Mitçǔ and is a complete physical row.
Mittei is deciding or determining secretly, with hisoka ni sadamuru providing the Japanese explanation. The Portuguese infinitive phrase continues below.
Completes the act of determining something in secret. The final upright S. is the dictionary's written-usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese sentence.
Mitzoo is glossed by hisoka ni kakusu, hiding something privately. The Portuguese shifts to the valued object kept secret; the printed spelling and caron are retained.

runs.text: ſecreta em muita estima como liuro, ou carta-

lines.note: The object is secretly kept in high esteem, with a book or notebook as examples. Carta- continues into cartapacio on the following physical row.
Pacio completes cartapacio; curiosities or treasured objects extend the examples. The closing S. is upright and marks written usage.

Miwake means distinguishing by sight. The example starts Iẽ-, representing zen with consonantal I and a nasal abbreviation; the following row supplies to aku, the contrast between good and evil. The small tilde is retained rather than the OCR's Iã.

Continues Iẽ-to aku to no futatsu wo akiraka ni miwake: clearly distinguishing the two, good and evil. The attached particles and the printed futatçuuo are preserved rather than respaced as modern Japanese.
Saxerareta completes the Japanese verb phrase; the Portuguese renders it as having clearly distinguished. Mon. is an upright citation label, followed by the italic translation.
The objects of discernment are good and evil, completing both the Portuguese sentence and the Japanese contrast begun three rows above.
Mi-wasure is forgetting what one has seen, directly matched by esquecer-se do que vio. The printed long s in the Japanese headword is retained.

runs.text: Vista ao longe ou ao comprido.

lines.note: Miwatashi here is the noun for a distant or extended view. The immediately following entry gives the corresponding verb rather than repeating this nominal definition.
The principal forms describe looking into the distance; -aita is the supplied historical past ending. Faru- begins the illustrative expression across the physical line break.
Farucano mucaiuo mivataxeba describes looking toward what lies far opposite. The printed Farucano is not normalized to Farucani; Mon. remains the upright citation label, including its terminal point.

runs.text: Vẽdo o que eſtà de fronte muito ao lõge.

lines.note: The translation says that one sees what is facing one a great distance away. The abbreviation tildes in Vẽdo and lõge and the grave in eſtà remain unexpanded.

runs.text: Interior dos paços, ou caſas de peſ-

lines.note: Miuchi first denotes the inner part of a noble residence or palace. The divided peſ- belongs to the Portuguese word peſſoas on the next line.

runs.text: ſoas nobres. ¶ Item, aliquando, a ſenhora da

lines.note: The residence belongs to noble people; a second, occasional sense identifies the lady of the house. Aliquando is explanatory Latin within the italic apparatus.
Completes that second sense as the household's lady or a lord's wife. The historical Portuguese spelling molher is not modernized.
Miuchixu refers respectfully to a household's people or retainers. The gloss begins to specify the honorific manner of referring to them.
Honra and reuerencia complete the indication that this designation of retainers is respectful. The row does not begin a new entry.

runs.text: Canal, q̃ eſtà nos rios, ou enſeadas poron-

lines.note: Miuo is a navigable channel in a river or inlet. The abbreviation q̃ stands unexpanded, and poron- continues into poronde on the next physical row.

runs.text: de as Funes vão deſuiandoſe dos baxos.

lines.note: Boats follow the channel while avoiding shoals. Funes is a Japanese boat term embedded, with a Portuguese plural ending, in the Portuguese explanation; its printed italic treatment is retained.

runs.text: Paos, ou eſtacas q̃ metem pera co-

lines.note: Miuogui denotes poles or stakes installed to identify the channel. The divided co- belongs to conhecer below, not to a Japanese example.
Nhecer o canal completes the purpose of the stakes: recognizing the channel. Although a continuation, this physical row begins close to the column margin, as in the baseline.
Miwokuri means following a departing person with one's eyes. The printed principal parts u, utta and the visible spacing A companhar are kept rather than regularized.
Ao que ſe vai supplies the person who is leaving, completing the visual-accompaniment definition. This is not a general escorting-on-foot gloss.
Miwoki is leaving something seen or having observed it well. The following example emphasizes experience retained from earlier events.
Mukashi no koto wo miwoita hito describes a person who has seen things of former times. The Portuguese begins Homem que, abbreviated as Homẽ q̃ in the print.

runs.text: tem viſto, ou paſſado por couſas antiguas, &

lines.note: Such a person has witnessed or lived through old events. Paſſado por supplies experience in addition to merely having seen something.
De muitos annos completes the reference to events many years old. The separate short line remains attached to the example under Mivoqi.

runs.text: Ver de lugar alto pera baixo.

lines.note: Miworoshi, with its supplied principal forms, means looking down from a high place. The next rows extend this spatial sense figuratively to contempt.

runs.text: ¶ Item, permet. Olhar a alguem com deſprezo.

lines.note: The figurative extension is looking at someone with contempt. The compressed printed permet. is retained rather than expanded into an editorial explanation in the transcription.
Hito wo choccato miworosu illustrates looking down on someone; Idem refers to the contemptuous sense immediately above. The printed adverb is retained without imposing a modern equivalent.
Mivooru is equated with miwowaru and mimakaru and glossed as dying. The explicit death gloss keeps this entry distinct from a verb meaning simply to finish looking.
The gloss adds coming to an end, then begins mivooru made wasururu koto. The following prohibition means not forgetting until life's end; this row is visibly indented.

runs.text: Não vos eſqueçais tè ofim da vida.

lines.note: Nakare completes the negative injunction: do not forget until the end of life. The printed tè and the joined ofim are preserved in the Portuguese rendering.

Miotoshi first means noticing a fault with the eyes, not only the modern familiar sense of overlooking something. The scan prints the abbreviated principal part u, without a secure preceding s; that anomaly is retained.

runs.text: falta, ou deſordẽ dalguem. ¶ Item, Ver

lines.note: The noticed object is someone's fault or disorder. A second sense begins with Ver and continues the idea of judging someone less favorably.

runs.text: com algum abatimento, ou menos conceito da

lines.note: This second sense involves a lowering of regard or a lesser opinion. The object of that changed judgment follows on the next row.

runs.text: peßoa do que tinha dantes. ¶ Item, Deixar

lines.note: The person is regarded less highly than before. The next Item opens the separate sense of failing to see something, so the apparently opposing meanings are genuinely distinguished by the dictionary.

runs.text: de ver por erro algũa couſa que deuera aduer-

lines.note: The third sense is overlooking by mistake something that should have been noticed. The visible aduer- continues into aduertir on the following row.

runs.text: tir, como algum bom lanço do jogo que hum

lines.note: Tir completes aduertir, and a good move in a game supplies the example of a missed opportunity. This is still the third sense of Mivotoxi.
The player has let that opportunity pass. This completes the body text of the first column; no body line or catchword follows beneath it.
Mivooxe is finishing seeing something completely. The scan prints Acabar do ver, including do rather than expected de; that grammatical irregularity is preserved.
Feitamente completes perfeitamente, explaining that the seeing is brought fully to completion. The short continuation is a separate physical row.
Mivoye denotes a tree grown from seed. The headword's v is clear on enlargement, correcting Miroye; the figurative extension begins at the line end.
Per-met. introduces the example kono mono wa waga ie no mioe, comparing a person with something grown in the household. The final copula is deferred to the next row.
Gia completes the Japanese predication; the Portuguese explains that this young man was born in the household. It is the figurative application of the seed-grown tree, not another botanical sense.
Mivoyobi means seeing or managing to see. Enlargement gives Mivoyobi, without the spurious extra ij in the OCR; the past ending ôda carries a circumflex.
Mivxinai is miushinai, losing sight of something; v before x represents the vowel u. The scan supports v rather than the OCR's y, and both supplied long-o marks are carons.

runs.text: O plantar de ſemente, ou carouço.

lines.note: Mivye denotes planting from a seed or fruit stone. This is related to, but distinct from, the earlier entry for a tree that has grown from seed.
Mivyeuo suru illustrates performing that planting. The Portuguese repeats the seed-based method and continues with another word for a seed below.
The alternative depeuide refers to planting from a pip or seed. Its joined spelling is retained, as is the historical u in peuide.
Mixe is showing something. The historical principal form ſuru is actually printed and is not silently converted to uru or a modern miseru paradigm.

runs.text: Tenda, partileiro, ou taboa em que ſe-

lines.note: Mixe as a noun is a stall, shelf, or board on which goods are displayed for sale. Tenda belongs wholly to the italic Portuguese explanation; the isolated roman T was an OCR styling error.
Goods are placed on the stall or display board for sale. The Japanese example begins Mixe- and continues with the object particle on the next physical row.
Mixeuo dasu means setting up a stall or display shelf. The scan repeats partileiro with r, not the OCR's partileito; Mi- begins the contrasting removal example.
Mixewo toriwoku, alternatively fazzusu, describes taking the stall away. The Japanese alternatives are examples, not embedded terms in the Portuguese prose.
Manchar completes desmanchar: dismantling the stall. It closes the removal example under the noun Mixe.
Miseburakashi means displaying something and then concealing it. The principal part aita is retained as the historical inflection provided in the entry.

runs.text: ſa, & eſcondela, como fazem a os mininos.

lines.note: The thing is shown and hidden as people do when teasing small children. The historical mininos and the separately printed a os are preserved.
Misedana is a stall or shelf used for displaying merchandise. Unlike Mixe above, this entry explicitly names the display furniture as a compound.
Couſas de venda supplies the goods put on that shelf. This is a short continuation of Mixedana rather than an independent entry.

runs.text: Catana que ſe mostra ao que ma-

lines.note: Misegatana is a sword displayed to a condemned person. The explanation continues across ma- and the following row, rather than defining an ordinary decorative sword.

runs.text: tão por juſtiça, pera que o cortem à vontade

lines.note: The person is being executed judicially; the displayed sword enables the actual blow to be delivered conveniently. The location of that blow follows below.
The executioner strikes from behind with another sword. Mixegatanauo suru then illustrates performing this threatening display.

runs.text: Fazer este medo, & moſtra cõ a Catana.

lines.note: The translation describes making this frightening display with the sword. Catana is embedded in the Portuguese sentence and retains its observed italic treatment.
Mishin denotes the outstanding balance of tribute, revenue, or obligatory service. The unpaid or unperformed nature of that balance is explained on the following rows.

runs.text: outro ſeruiço obrigatorio que fica por fazer, ou

lines.note: The balance can be another obligatory service still to be performed or paid. Obrigatorio is a single printed word; the OCR's internal split obligator io is removed.
Mishin wo nasu, alternatively sumasu, means discharging the outstanding obligation. The Portuguese Cõ begins cumprir across the line boundary without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: prir com esta diuida, ou resto que ficou.

lines.note: Prir completes Cõprir, followed by the debt or balance that remains. The continuation is retained without expanding the abbreviation or changing diuida to modern spelling.
Mishin ga aru or nokoru means that an obligation remains outstanding. These two Japanese alternatives share the following Portuguese explanation.

The remaining work is still to be done. The next example starts with upright O-, the first syllable of Oracio on the next row; the OCR had wrongly absorbed it into italic prose and read its hyphen as a point.
Oracio no mishin applies the same outstanding-balance expression to prayers. Oracio is part of the Japanese example here, not an isolated Portuguese explanation; the translation begins Resto.

runs.text: raçoẽs que hum cuſtuma a rezar.

lines.note: Completes the reference to prayers that a person customarily recites but has not yet finished. The printed raçoẽs preserves the tilde on e.
Mishiri is knowing or recognizing; the damaged final i of Mixiri is visible, unlike the shortened OCR Mixir. Mi wo mi- begins the example about knowing oneself.
Xiru completes mi wo mishiru, glossed as knowing oneself. The Portuguese aſi meſmo retains the printed joined aſi rather than modern a si.
Mishoo here means not yet born, explained by imada umarezu. Its caron distinguishes it graphically from the following entry with a circumflex.
Mishoo ijen means before birth. The example repeats the caron of the headword and should not inherit the different accent in Mixô below.
Mixô is smiling or laughing a little, explained by sukoshi waroo. The headword has a circumflex while varǒ has a caron; upright S. marks written usage.
Miya denotes a shrine of the kami. The Portuguese uses ermida as its explanatory category and the pluralized Japanese Camis within the gloss.

runs.text: Filho do Rey. ¶ Itẽ, Seus paços.

lines.note: A separate Miya entry denotes a royal son and, by extension, his palace. The second sense is explicitly introduced by the abbreviated Item.

runs.text: Molher de quem o Rey ouue al-

lines.note: Miyabara refers to a woman by whom the ruler has had a child. The qualifying exclusion that defines her status continues below.

runs.text: gum filho, que não he Rainha.

lines.note: The woman is not the queen. This completes the status distinction in Miyabara rather than excluding the child from the definition.
Miyabito is equated with kugetachi, court nobles. The Portuguese divides fidalgos after fi- across the physical line break.

runs.text: dalgos que ſeruem ao Dairi no paço.

lines.note: Those nobles serve the Dairi at the palace. Dairi occurs inside the Portuguese explanation, whereas Cuguetachi above is a Japanese synonym and is not a typeface-toggle candidate.

runs.text: Cidade onde està a corte do Rey.

lines.note: Miyako is the city in which the ruler's court is located. The definition is functional and does not insert a specific city name absent from the print.
This Miyama is a bird name, with Miyamajitoto given as the preferred expression. Meliùs is italic editorial Latin; the Japanese alternative remains upright.
Nho completes Paßarinho, a small bird so called. The gloss does not itself provide a secure modern species identification.
The next Miyama is explained by fukai yama, a deep or densely wooded mountain. The Portuguese mui- continues into muito below.

To completes muito: the mountain's woodland is very thick. The separate far-right Miya- anticipates Miyamagacure on f0325 and has been moved to a catchword zone, not discarded or included in the running definition.
